speechtext:
Last year, at the request of the right hon. gentleman who is now leader of the government, I was asked to produce a personal letter that was not on the public file but on the minister's file. The contention
Motions I or Papers

was that, although marked "personal," it was acted on :by the minister, and that such a letter should be produced. These are the very words:
A personal letter written to a minister about a personal matter and placed upon his personal file is privileged, and this house has so ruled. But a letter marked "personal" which deals with the public business of Canada cannot be made personal merely by marking it so. That principle has been laid down by parliament from the first time the production of papers was called for, because parliament claims the right to redress grievances and it claims the right to know what the grievances are before supply is granted.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-RIVIERE DU LOUP STATION

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-RIVIERE DU LOUP STATION
speechtext:
I wholly agree with the observations of the hon. member for Gloucester that no exception should be made in the application of the rule. The letter to which he refers was a letter, knowledge of the existence of which came into being through a letter which was on the file produced. It thus came to the attention of those who had the file that such a letter had been written about the public business and therefore it was producible; but the principle has not been changed in the least that personal correspondence is not in any sense to be brought down. It never has been and I suppose it never will be in any parliament. The hon. gentleman may say that it was on a minister's own file, but what happened in that case is no evidence of what may have happened in this. In that case in the file brought down there was reference to a letter. We asked where the letter was. The then minister said: It is on my personal file. We said: As the correspondence shows it was acted upon as a public document, obviously it must be produced as such. That is all. I am of the same opinion still. But the question whether or not a man has the right to mark a letter as "personal" is quite clear; it has never been challenged in parliament. It arose very acutely in the 1926 campaign as to whether a letter marked "personal" could be brought down, could be shown. The consensus of opinion was that the writer was the

judge of the character of the communication; that he had the right to maintain the personal character of his communication, and that until he gave his consent the recipient could not make public the contents. That is the position, as far as I understand it, and everything I said on that occasion I would repeat now. If by any chance any letter is shown by the file to be a letter that, although marked "personal," is referred to by the minister in the action he takes, I would still hold to the view I then expressed, and say that it should be produced on the public record.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-RIVIERE DU LOUP STATION
speechtext:
On the point of order,
I would say that whether or not those papers should be tabled, is a matter for argument. The house has the right to refuse such a motion and it has done so in the past; but that is not a question of order. Any member has the right to ask for these documents; it is not against the rules to ask for them. The government may take the responsibility of asking that the motion be refused, but not of asking you to rule it out of order, Mr. Speaker, because it is not out of order.

maintopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL RAILWAYS-RIVIERE DU LOUP STATION
speechtext:
Just before the subject of correspondence is left, if it is a proper moment at which to refer to it, I think that a distinction must be made between what is personal in the sense in which personal communications are generally so understood, and what is personal only in the sense of avoiding publication of the reply. For example, if a communication is addressed to a minister of the crown on a public matter, his reply to that communication should be available for publication equally with the original communication. Otherwise, ministers of the crown may evade answering in a public way questions on public matters. I raise the point more particularly because I believe it is true that with respect to a very considerable amount of the correspondence that has taken place since the present administration came into office, replies made by ministers of the crown to public communications, have been marked "personal". The reply in no sense, strictly speaking, was personal. It was an answer on the part of a member of the government to a public communication, and there should not be afforded to the ministry the possibility of evading the publication of their replies to public communications simply by marking them "personal." If, however, a minister wishes to communicate on a personal matter, certainly he can mark his letter "personal", and a personal communication in that sense would be respected, but on a public matter where an individual writes

to the government and expects to receive an official acknowledgment, and receives that acknowledgment on government paper signed by the minister, the word "personal" written on the corner of the letter should not in any sense protect it from publicity. I think that that is the sound view.
Speaking on the same matter with respect to private secretaries, the private secretary's reply is the reply of the minister. The private secretaries are civil servants, and communications signed by private secretaries should not in any way be privileged. They must stand on all fours with communications from the ministers. A letter from a private secretary is in exactly the same position as a letter from a minister and should be regarded as such.

If the right hon. gentleman had followed the decisions in the courts he would realize that the problem is not as simple as he suggests. The action of McIntosh vs. Dunn, which went to the privy council from Australia, is the leading authority upon the subject. I happen to recall it at the moment. There are other cases of the same kind. The question of privilege, when set up by the recipient of a letter, and the publication of it with respect to a claim for damages for libel, raises issues that I shall not take the time of this house to discuss, but I think that this is a fair rule. I think the right hon. gentleman has stated it too broadly. The right of any minister to write a personal letter to a correspondent I think cannot be denied. If the correspondent seeks information of a public character the minister may turn the letter over to one of his staff, to a secretary, and see that he gets a reply. If the correspondent writes a letter seeking some information about a very ordinary, everyday transaction, and the minister in reply says, "For your personal information I can only inform you such and such," certainly it seems to me he should be able to protect himself and make that a personal communication by marking it "personal," not for the purpose of evading anything, but for the purpose of carrying on, if he desires, a friendly correspondence with anyone who addresses him in a personal way, for the purpose of ascertaining certain facts.
Motions for Papers

Certainly I have seen enough correspondence of former ministers, now sitting on the other side, during their tenure of office to know that the word "personal" was used very frequently on many communications that were received by their correspondents, sometimes by myself, in answer to inquiries that I had made, and in my judgment that word was quite properly put there. As the right hon. gentleman knows, cable communications that pass between different governments are marked "confidential," and, for reasons that are good and sufficient, they cannot be brought down in this house without the consent of the other government. Whether marked "confidential" or not, the consent of the other government should first be obtained before bringing them down. Broadly, the question is one of maintenance of good faith between people who carry on a correspondence. If one has written the letter in good faith on a personal and confidential matter, he has the right to have it so treated if he marks it as such. But on the other hand, if the letter is sent for the purpose of public attention being directed thereto and reference being made to it publicly, it does not come within that rule.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR LOSS OR RENUNCIATION OF CANADIAN NATIONALITY

speechtext:
Hon. C. H. CAHAN (Secretary of State) moved the second reading of Bill No. 24, to define Canadian nationals and to provide for loss or renunciation of Canadian nationality.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take much of the time of the house in a discussion of this bill. I think we have reached the stage in the evolution of our national life when we should seriously consider the foundations for its future development. For sixty-four years we have had a very satisfactory material development. We have been promoting great national works, carving out new provinces, providing organized govern-
Canadian Nationals Act

ment for the great Northwest Territories, and I think we have succeeded far 'beyond the expectations of the fathers of confederation in the material and commercial development of Canada. In connection with that development, however, if we are to assume the status of a nation within the British commonwealth, we must also assume very serious duties and responsibilities. Among the responsibilities resting upon the parliament of Canada is that of framing a clear definition of "Canadian nationals" for whom the government and parliament are responsible, whether they be resident in the dominion or temporarily resident outside our territorial jurisdiction. So long as they retain the status of Canadian nationals they should in my opinion be treated as such and as holding a status within the dominion equal to that which any others individually enjoy.
When the Treaty of Versailles was signed certain articles related to Canadian nationals. The matter came to my personal attention because of the fact that many hundreds, who were applicants for compensation for damages suffered by illegal enemy warfare, necessarily were compelled to prove before the commissioner appointed to hear evidence that they were Canadian nationals at the time the Treaty of Versailles was ratified. In proving that they were such Canadian nationals they were compelled to resort for a definition to the Immigration Act, which was drawn not for the express purpose of defining the term "Canadian nationals", but rather for the purpose of defining those who are not admissible to this country as immigrants. It seemed to me a matter of regret that in dealing with the status of Canadian nationals we should be compelled to resort to an enactment which was put on the statute book as an act respecting immigration, for the purpose of providing measures for keeping people out of this country.
Then a further serious question was brought frequently to my notice. We have in this country hundreds of thousands of immigrants who have obtained certificates of naturalization, and who are settled here and who by reason of the fact that they have become domiciled British subjects are, within the meaning of the present act, "Canadian nationals." But if any of those immigrants who have obtained naturalization certificates-some of them members of this parliament-happen to be out of this country for a year, for instance, on a voyage around the world, or on a visit to Argentina to attend the British Empire fair, and through illness are not able

to return home within the year, those Canadian nationals, simply by reason of that absence, although British subjects, are, under the existing acts prevented from reentering Canada and from resuming their domicile here, except they do so subject to the same objections as if they were coming in anew from Siberia, Kamchatka, Turkestan or some other foreign country, and had never been subjects of the king, domiciled in Canada. It seems to me that these surprising difficulties should be dealt with by an act of parliament clearly defining who are Canadian nationals.
Take another case. During the short time that I have occupied the position of Secretary of State I think there is not a religious organization in Canada engaged in missionary work in foreign countries that has not brought before the Department of State questions as to the national status of its missionaries in Japan, China or India whio were formerly domiciled in Canada, but who have remained outside of this country for more than a year, and who have married and had children born to them in those countries. Under the present law some of those missionaries have no right -I make that assertion subject to correction, but it has been so decided I think-have no right to return to this country with their wives and children simply because under the existing law they are not Canadian nationals in the sense that they retain the right to return to Canada and resume the domicile which they left temporarily to represent great Canadian religious institutions in foreign countries.
Since I assumed the office of Secretary of State, representatives by the score, Canadians abroad, commercial agents, men sent abroad for the purpose of performing public duties and public service on behalf of the government of Canada, have raised the question as to whether their wives and their children bom abroad are to be deemed Canadian nationals. If they are Canadian nationals as defined by the parliament, of Canada, then I take the ground that it is the duty and responsibility of this parliament to enact that those Canadian nationals shall have the right to return to their former domicile and take up their lives in this country as from the time they left Canada on foreign service or to represent our great religious institutions, or other institutions dealing with trade, commerce and industry, which to successfully perform their functions abroad must have trade agents and representatives in foreign countries.
If this bill is to pass in its present form it seems clear that there must be amendments to it or to the Immigration Act. Therefore it may be difficult to proceed with the bill in

Canadian Nationals Act
committee of the whole house. But I should like, and I think the government of the day would like, to have an expression of opinion from hon. members as to whether, for the preservation of our own self-respect, for the maintenance of our dignity as a young nation, and to lay the foundations for our future national life, the time has not come when we are bound to define, as clearly as concise language may permit, who are Canadian nationals, with a view to fulfilling our duties and responsibilities to those Canadians temporarily resident abroad who should have equal status with ourselves in this country.
I should like this bill to receive second reading. As to whether it should go to a select committee or should be dealt with in committee of the whole house, I am at present in doubt. Therefore if the bill is read a second time I should like to have it reserved.
Of course, I have received protests against this bill, especially from the province of British Columbia, on the ground that under its terms one of the Japanese or Chinese race who was born in British Columbia would thereby become a Canadian national. But in that respect I wish to say that this bill makes no change whatever in the existing law. Whether a person be of the Chinese, the Japanese, the Malay or the Indian race, that person, male or female, born in this country thereby becomes a British subject, and if domiciled in this country thereby becomes a Canadian national under the law as it at present exists. I repeat, no change is proposed in that respect.
Therefore I submit the bill for the sympathetic consideration, I hope, of the house, because, speaking for myself, I am as proud as any other man of being a Canadian national born and bred in this country, but I shall be prouder still of my own people when 'by the laws we place upon the statute book and by our administration of those laws we make it clear that a Canadian national shall continue to be a Canadian national unless, by his own overt act he severs his connection with this country and refuses to continue his status as a Canadian national for the future.

I do not wish to speak at any length on the bill, but I may observe that with the principle of it we on this side of the house, or at least a large proportion of us, agree. This is not a new matter. It was brought before the house in 1921 by the Right Hon. Mr. Doherty, who was then Minister of Justice, and who had a bill passed covering the subject. The whole question was under study by the late administration of my right hon. leader (Mr. Mackenzie King), both in the Department of the Secretary of State, over which I had the honour to preside, and in the Department of External Affairs.
Reports have been asked from experts in the matter with respect to the international,

Canadian Nationals Act
legal and other points of view, and there is a vast amount of correspondence, besides other documents, with respect to the whole subject. This information, gathered by the two departments I have mentioned, is the product of years of effort to find a solution for this very interesting but most complex problem.	.
The principle underlying the bill is the endeavour to define what is a Canadian national as distinguished from a British subject. British subjects are defined in the Naturalization Act; and, as the house is aware, the conditions under which persons become British subjects by statute are decided, not in this Dominion alone but by agreement between the mother country and the various dominions. Certain conditions underlie the granting of certificates of naturalization to British subjects, one <of them being the condition just alluded to in the dialogue which took place after my hon. friend's speech on the question of residence. May I say that that residence clause in the Canadian statute is not exclusive to us, but it is one of the conditions upon which all the dominions and the mother country have agreed to in the granting of naturalization papers. The present bill does not deal with naturalization, it is simply a definition of what is to be a Canadian national, distinguishing a citizen of Canada from a citizen of Australia or New Zealand, although all are British subjects under another statute.
I hold in my hand a report on this very problem which was made to the Secretary of State by a learned professor in Toronto. I do not intend to quote very extensively from this report, but a passing allusion to it may clarify the situation. This professor suggested a definition of subjects of His Majesty peculiarly relating to their Canadian citizenship. The explanation given is that two conditions must be recognized: first, the fact that the Dominion of Canada is not an independent state according to the categories contained in international law, and, second, the fact that she possesses legal rights arising from her position under the crown and in international affairs which she can confer on certain persons or classes of persons. The term 'Canadian national was adopted both by my right hon. friend and by Right Hon. Mr. Doherty in 195S1, the contention being that it satisfies both, the idea of Canadian national autonomy and Canada's essential position in relation to the crown and the empire. In a way it is a cumbersome title but, as the expert says,
and I fully agree with him, no simple title will meet a complicated situation.
A bill was introduced and adopted by this house in 1921. I confess that I am basing my conclusions on the different reports which came before me since that time. The main difficulty with the bill introduced by the Right Hon. Mr. Doherty in 1921 was that the definition then made of a Canadian national was based on some other statute, namely, the Immigration Act. The bill of 1921 enumerated the classes of Canadian nationals, among them being any British subject who is a Canadian citizen within the meaning of the Immigration Act. There were other sections in that bill, but I allude only to that one.
In defining a Canadian national we should have a basic statute which independent of any other enactment should be complete and inclusive in itself. The Immigration Act deals with a special situation, that of admitting citizens into this country and I know -the Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan) will bear me out in this-that there has always been a great deal of difficulty in the administration of the Naturalization Act under the Secretary of State and the administration of the Immigration Act under some other department. If we follow the example set by the bill of 1921, and define a Canadian national as being a Canadian citizen as defined by the Immigration Act, we will be faced with further difficulty. I commend the attitude taken by the Secretary of State in endeavouring in his bill to define "Canadian national", not by a reference to any other statute but by making a basic statutory definition which will be complete within the borders of the bill.
The interchange of questions and answers which we heard just a moment ago on some of the complexities of this matter, and the doubt entertained by such a learned person as the Secretary of State, would lend strength to his suggestion that this bill be referred to a special committee of the house. We agree with the principle of the bill, affecting as it does a matter upon which the late administration had been working for some time. I will vote for the second reading. It is not within my province to move that the 'bill be referred to a special committee for consideration, but as the Secretary of State has invited suggestions on this point, I urge very strongly that the bill be sent to a special committee where the many difficulties and complexities connected therewith can be fully threshed out.

Mr. Speaker, I think this is one of the most important bills which has ever come before this house. I agree with the suggestion of the last speaker (Mr. Rinfret) that this bill should be referred to a special committee of [DOT]the house for very serious consideration. There is one subsection which should receive special attention, namely, subsection (f) of section 2, which reads:
"Natural-born British subject" means a natural-born British subject as defined in part I of the Naturalization Act.
This clause of the Naturalization Act provides that a person bom on a British ship, whether or not in territorial waters, becomes a British citizen, and if that subsection were adopted the same definition would be carried out in the present bill. Our naturalization laws should conserve for our own people the exclusive right to say who may become citizens of this country, but that right is not preserved in the present bill. By the provisions of the Naturalization Act a child bom in Canada or upon a British ship becomes a British subject, whether we like it or not, or whether children so born, or their parents, are fit persons to become citizens of Canada. I contend that the provisions of this bill should be changed to such an extent as not to extend this right to any child of alien parentage bom within His Majesty's dominions or on board a British ship, unless the parents of suich child are fit and proper persons, both physically and morally, to become naturalized citizens of this country.
Many undesirable people are making their way into this country, and I believe I am correct in saying that the state has the power to say who shall become its citizens. On the Pacific coast we are faced with a race problem. These newcomers will not assimilate with our Anglo-Saxon stock, and they are content with a much lower standard of living and of civilization. Their birth rate is much higher, and in this connection I should like to refer to the increase in the school population of orientals as against whites. Even if bars were put up against Asiatics coming into British Columbia, and such immigration ceased, the birth rate would still be alarming and in the course of years the Asiatic probably would overshadow the white population. There are some 54,000 orientals in British Columbia and last year the birth rate for Japanese alone was 38 per cent as against five per cent for whites. Steps should be taken immediately to conserve our heritage for our own people. When I speak of heritage I mean the land that these Asiatics are 
gradually beginning to control in British Columbia. The figures for last year, compiled by the Minister of Lands for British Columbia, show that some 50,000 acres are owned or controlled by members of the Japanese race.
The oriental problem has two sides, economic and national, but the national side is the most important. The Asiatic problem has been before the house many times, but I think this would be a good time to consider seriously whether or not we are to continue to allow such people who are not assimilable [DOT]to become Canadians. This question must be settled definitely sooner or later. At present it is probably primarily a British Columbia question, but it is a very serious question so far as our province is concerned.
For the benefit of the house I am going to recite briefly the history in connection with the situation out there. In 1908 the so-called gentleman's agreement with Japan was made by the Hon. Mr. Lemieux, whereby among other conditions it was agreed that Japan should limit immigrants of the domestic and agriculture types to 400 a year. Former residents of Canada and those coming to work under contract were also admitted. In 1910 the Immigration Act was amended to give the minister power to exclude any race deemed undesirable in Canada. In 1919 the act was further amended to give the minister power to reject those considered unsuitable for assimilation. This provision was not used against the Japanese. In 1913 the Anglo-Japanese treaty was adopted by Canada. It contained a clause allowing the nationals of other countries to live and trade in the country of each contracting party. Canada's adoption of the treaty was modified by a clause stating that nothing in the treaty should be held to affect the provisions of the Immigration Act. In 1923 negotiations with Japan modified the Lemieux agreement and cut the limit of domestics and agricultural labourers to be admitted to 150 instead of 400.
There is no specific law dealing with Japanese immigration. Canada acts simply under the agreement with Japan which undertakes to limit the number of pasports to those desiring to enter Canada, while Canada agrees to admit those with passports and to prohibit others from entering. In the years preceding 1927 the Japanese birth rate was over five times that of the white. Last year the Japanese population increased 74 per cent as against an increase of 6 per cent in the white population. Your oriental is no pioneer. He lets the white man open up the country. When it is organized he purchases

or leases improved land and reaps the reward. This is where uninformed eastern opinion goes astray. Otherwise why should they look on that problem as largely one of filling up our open spaces. I am not going to deal with the matter at greater length, because many figures have been given in connection with it; but the suggestion of the minister should be taken seriously and before we proceed much further with this bill it should be referred to a committee where this grave aspect of affairs in British Columbia should be 'taken into consideration.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT BY ORDER IN COUNCIL-AMENDMENT, MR. BOURASSA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before you leave the chair, I would ask the forbearance of the house to consider for a moment a matter of importance, especially in view of the comments that have been passed in the province of Quebec with regard to the adoption by the government of the order in council prohibiting the importation of Russian goods. I want, however, to enlarge the question and to discuss for a few moments the whole principle of government by order in council. In order to make my position clear, I shall read immediately the motion which I propose to move:
The house regards the growing practice of deciding by order in council important matters of public policy as an encroachment upon the duties and privileges of parliament and a violation of the principle of responsible government.
Ever since I have occupied a seat in the house-and that is thirty-five years ago-and even prior to that, I have heard leaders of the various oppositions criticize the then government for deciding by order in council matters which should be referred to parliament. I shall not dwell at length upon what might be called the academic aspect of the question; but nevertheless it seems to me that, especially since the war, the evolution of government in this as well as in other countries calls for serious reflection on the part of those who still hold faith in parliamentary and responsible institutions. I must say that my own faith has been somewhat shaken; but at the same time, so long as we pretend to be a country governed by parliamentary practices, so long as we claim that
the government of the day is but the executive committee of the House of Commons, we should be very careful about allowing the cabinet to carry on, by orders in council or even by private dictates of the Prime Minister, matters that ought to be threshed out in the house where the elected representatives of the people sit.
Of course I was bound by the rules of the house to give to this motion perhaps the appearance of a motion of want of confidence, but I want to say at once that it is not so much a motion of blame against the present government, as an expression, might I say, of criticism against a system that has been growing upon us and that has been pursued by practically all governments. In order to make my position clear, I am going to illustrate it by summing up before the house the case of our external relations, taking as a concrete example the relations between Canada and Russia during the last ten- years. I have chosen that particular question for two reasons, first, because in those ten years all our relations with Russia have been dealt with by. orders in council. Not in a single instance has a decision been taken by the Canadian government, whether by a Liberal or by a Conservative government, under the advice of the house, nor has the government received from the house any mandate to enter into or to break relations with Russia, or to change the basis of our relations with that country. In these days, especially since the war, when we are entering into the field of foreign affairs, whether for the making of trade agreements or of diplomatic arrangements, when we are beginning to have Canadian representatives accredited to foreign governments, it is of the highest importance that there should be an understanding whether our foreign relations, either diplomatic or commercial, are going to be determined by parliament or by the government without consultation of parliament. That is my second reason.
Three years ago I gave a part of the story which I am bound to repeat to-day, in order to complete my argument. As may be remembered by some members of the house, in 1921, a trade agreement was concluded between the British government and the government of the Soviet republic. This trade agreement was not made by a labour-radical cabinet, but by the coalition government presided over by Mr. Lloyd George. It was signed by a staunch, respectable Conservative member of that government, Sir Robert Horne, and on behalf of Russia by Mr. Krassin, who, I think, according to all testimony, was one of the most respectable-I hope there were others-mem-
Embargo on Russian Goods

bers of the Russian government. This trade agreement was concluded, in the very terms of the white paper which I have in my hand, "pending the conclusion of a formal general peace treaty between Great Britain and Russia."
It contains various clauses defining, for example, the conditions under which the nationals of the two countries should live in their respective territories, concerning the protection of the rights and facilities necessary to enable the people of both countries to carry on trade, and so forth. It contemplated the appointment of official agents of each government to the other. This agreement was concluded on the 16th of March, 1921. I am now going to quote from various papers produced during the session of 1928, under numbers 180 A, B and C of the sessional papers of that year.
On the 22nd of August, 1921, an order in council was passed by the Canadian government upon the recommendation of the then Minister of Trade and Commerce, Sir George Poster, with no bolshevist tendencies, I believe, in these terms:
The minister recommends that His Majesty's government-
The government in England-
-be informed that Canada desires to participate in the arrangement for the resumption of trade with Russia.
That was referring to the agreement concluded in the month of March. The order in council was communicated by Lord Byng to the then Secretary of State for the Colonies, Mr. Churchill, on the 30th of August. Some previous despatch must have been sent, because on the 25th of August, Mr. Gregory, who was, I think, Under Secretary of Foreign Affairs in England, had already written to Mr. Berzin, chief of the Russian delegation in London, as follows:
I am directed by the Marquess Curzon of Kedleston-
Another one, I believe, not under any suspicion of bolshevism-
-to inform you that the Canadian government has expressed the desire to be associated with His Majesty's government in the trade agreement between Russia and Great Britain.
Mind you, Mr. Speaker, there was no question of restraining the relations of Canada and Russia merely to trade matters. What the Canadian government asked for was to be associated with the government of Great Britain in all the terms of what I might call this preface to a formal peace treaty between Great Britain and Russia. Some correspond-

ence ensued and on October 15, 1921, Mr. Churchill wrote to Lord Byng a despatch in which a form, of the adhesion of Canada to that treaty was suggested. The form is this:
The government of the Dominion of Canada having expressed their desire that the provisions of the agreement between the government of the United Kingdom and the Russian Soviet government for the resumption of trade and commerce between the two countries which was signed at London on the 16th day of March, 1921. should apply also to Canada and to merchandise, the produce and manufacture of Canada, it is hereby agreed that the provisions of that agreement shall as and* from the date of the present agreement-
Meaning the agreement to be made by Canada-	[DOT]
-be held to apply to the Dominion of Canada and to govern the relations between Canada and Russia.
Not only trade relations between Canadian dealers and Russian tradesmen, but relations between Canada as a state and the Soviet republic as another State. Evidently the matter was considered favourably by the Canadian government because on the 26th of December, 1921, upon a report from the Secretary of State for External Affairs, who was then the Prime Minister, Mr. Arthur Meighen. an order in council was passed by the Canadian government in the following terms:
The committee of the privy council have had before them a report dated 17th of December, 1921, from the Right Hon. the Secretary of State for External Affairs

Mr. Meighen-
[DOT]-to whom was referred a despatch from the Right Hon. the Secretary of State for the Colonies, dated 15th of October, 1921, regarding the desire of the Canadian government to participate in the arrangement for the resumption of trade with Russia, proposing a formula to be embodied in notes to be exchanged between the foreign office and the Russian trade delegation with the object of making applicable to Canada the provisions of the trade agreement between the government of the United Kingdom and the Russian Soviet government, and inquiring whether Your Excellency's ministers would concur in the terms of such formula. The minister, with the concurrence of the Minister of Trade and Commerce-
Again, I repeat, Sir George Foster-
[DOT]-states that the proposed formula is approved by the Canadian government.
The committee on the recommendation of the Right Hon. the Secretary of State for External Affairs advise that Your Excellency may be pleased to inform the Right Hon. the Secretary of State for the Colonies to this effect by telegraph.
All of which is respectfully submitted for Your Excellency's approval.
(Signed) Rodolphe Boudreau,
Clerk of the Privy Council.

Embargo on Russian Goods
To show the house the importance which the then Conservative government attached to getting into close trade and political and friendly relations with the Russian government, which has been styled both in and out of this house as a government of atheists and murderers, this order in council was passed, I would point out, twenty days after the Conservative government had been defeated at the polls and just three days before they resigned. Practically the last action of importance that was taken by that government was to make sure that Canada would not lose her chance of entering into friendly relations with the Soviet government. I am not saying that in any spirit of criticism or sarcasm, but simply to demonstrate on what a fragile basis rest the comments that have been made recently in the province of Quebec with regard to our relations with Russia. The Soviet government with which the Canadian government made that agreement was much more directly concerned, either as a government or through its personnel, with the murder of the czar, the czarina and their children than the present Russian government. Mr. Lenin was still the chief of that government, and the foreign minister was still Mr. Chicherin. The representative of the Soviet in London was Mr. Krassin. Mr. Krassin had no share in the responsibility for events of October, 1917. But the government with which Canada entered into friendly relations was a government certainly as, if not more, communistic than that with , which by order in council of a few months ago we broke relations. At the present time I am not expressing my opinion as to the propriety of one action or the other, but am simply pointing out the facts.
Three days after this important document was passed and after the arrangement had been made, a change took place in the government of Canada. The Liberal party was called to power. They concluded the accord, in other words, they affixed their signatures to the document which had been prepared by Mr. Meighen upon the suggestion of Sir George Foster, and it was sent to London. what happened at that time. Various demands had been made in London to bring about a cessation of the relations with Russia. The previous Labour government had refused. I shall quote from his communication:
Especially as the Soviet action which has led to the present situation is directed against institutions of all parts of the British empire, we should like to suggest for consideration that as regards the retention of Soviet representatives this is a matter on which uniformity of action by the various members of the commonwealth concerned would present great advantages.
To this communication the then Governor General, Lord Willingdon, in the name of his ministers, replied in these very significant terms:
The despatches received from London do not indicate that any documents have been found in the Arcos raid -which establish that the official agency in Canada has been a centre of espionage and subversive propaganda. If any evidence to this effect has been discovered, it is desired to be informed as early as possible. It is further desired to learn whether His Majesty's government in Great Britain, in terminating the trade agreement, are acting under paragraph 1 of article 13 of the agreement, providing for six month's notice, or under paragraph 3, providing for immediate termination in the event of an infringement, and in the latter case whether any special steps have been taken towards giving the other party an opportunity of furnishing an explanation.

Here we have the assertion by the Governor General of Canada that no case of espionage had been detected in Canada, and that therefore Canada as a nation had no reason to break the arrangement. To that communication the Secretary of State replied:
Such information as was obtained from Arcos raid directly relating to Canada consisted of addresses found in possession of Anton Miller.
Curiously enough most of the addresses were found to be located in the loyal city of Toronto, and the names mentioned were of good Anglo Saxon origin. No mention was made in the despatch concerning the activities of those persons, nor was any mention made of any subversive propaganda being carried on in Canada. Without waiting for further evidence, on the 26th May, the day following the despatch from Mr. Amery, the Governor General wired the following to the Secretary of State for Dominion Affairs:
So far as Canada is concerned there has been a steady and substantial growth of trade under the agreement and there has not been any substantial ground of complaint as to espionage or propaganda against the present official agent in Canada.
Of course, the reference here was to the Russian agent.
My ministers have concluded that the evidences of espionage and subversive propaganda set forth by your Prime Minister make it clear that an essential condition of the agreement as entered into by Canada as well as Great Britain, namely, that each party should "refrain from hostile action or undertakings and from conducting outside of its own borders any official propaganda direct or indirect against the institutions of the British Empire," has not been fulfilled. In order to remove any doubt as to whether the agreement lapses automatically and having regard to all the circumstances, they have accordingly decided to terminate the agreement.
So that as the matter then stood, Mr. Speaker, after the Canadian government had admitted and asserted officially and unreservedly that no evidence of communistic propaganda had been found in Canada, before they had received even the text of the speeches delivered in the Imperial House of Commons, they terminated our agreement with Russia-again by order in council. But they left private individuals still free to deal with each other as they thought fit and under the ordinary risks of trade between two countries that have no special treaties or trade agreements, but are not at war with each other. sensus of opinion of all was this: What brought about the extraordinary success of bolshevism was the defects, the vices of the regime which preceded it. I do not mean czardom alone. I would put it broadly as lack of responsibility on the part of the leading classes, whether czar, bureaucrats, or noble absentees, spending on the Riviera by millions money gathered from the peasantry of Russia with whom they had no contact. The absenteeism of the landowners was the curse of Ireland for centuries; it was the curse of France in the century and a half which preceded the French revolution. What prevented England during her great upheaval from falling into the same abyss into which France fell 140 or 150 years later, or into which Russia fell a few years ago, was that the English landlords, with all their defects, their narrowness of mind and class spirit, at least lived on their lands. They fulfilled some of the social functions and duties for which they had received their privileges. The English merchants w'ere patriotic; they were sometimes narrow and sometimes grafting in their trade relations, but when the nation came to a crisis they were generous in the disposal of their wealth in order to help out their country. At times they espoused the cause of the people against the king; at times they sustained the authority of the king; but with their faults and mistakes they at least, to the best of their knowledge, fulfilled their social functions. In any country, especially in every large country where you have an immense population that has been groaning for centuries, deprived of the elements of comfort and civilization, and where you have a privileged class enjoying all the privileges and not fulfilling its duties, there is bound to be revolution. In 1929 they paid a dividend equivalent to 50 per cent on the share capital. This year the surplus of their assets over their liabilities has decreased from $62,000,000 to $33,000,000, a decrease of $29,000,000. Their reserve for doubtful stock has been decreased from $12,500,000 to about $5,000,000. On the other hand, they increased their capital investment in their enormous and monstrous building in Montreal from $11,000,000 to $23,000,000, and they have raised their dividends to their shareholders to 75 per cent of the capital. Now I ask, in the face of such things, are we entitled to teach lessons in Christianity and social order to other countries, when during last winter we had thousands and thousands of fathers of families not capable of purchasing a pound of bread for their children, receiving alms from charitable institutions and from city councils, and when we have hundreds of thousands of children raised in Montreal in dwellings that are not fit for human beings? When we see such a monstrous concentration of capital, when we see especially that unchristian and unsocial creation of fictitious capital, which you and I and every other consumer of food or clothing or any other human need, have to pay for, do you not think, sir, that it is about time that we should look to ourselves and put some degree of Christianity into our own social and economic polity be-
fore we launch a crusade against coal and pulpwood, but not including wheat, because there are too many farmers in the west who want to sell wheat? Joseph Chamberlain, in the days that preceded the alliance of Great Britain and Russia, when he was trying to make a bargain with Germany in order to crush France and Russia, speaking of the barbarous Russian, said, "If you want to sup with the devil, you must use a long spoon." We do not want to sup or dine or breakfast with the devil as far as coal is concerned, because it may hurt Senator Webster's trade. We do not want to take Russian pulpwood because it may endanger the speculative stocks of Sir Herbert Holt. In. order however to relieve the sufferings of our northwestern friends we are prepared to breakfast, dine, sup and take the last cup with those devils, with very short spoons, and even to drink from the same glass with them, as I think Mr. Ferguson has done this week.
I do not think there is any necessity to dwell further upon this subject. I thought it was my duty to discuss the matter for several reasons, one of which is that I am an old man. I have not much to risk; my political future is rather limited. My principles and ideals are well known both in my province and outside. I have put up many a battle, perhaps wrongly at times, for what I thought to be my duty to my country. Throughout those battles may I say without boasting I always had in mind two guiding thoughts. Whatever my faults and mistakes may have been I have never sacrificed what I thought to be my convictions as a Catholic, my duty to my race or to my country. But more than anything else I have hated the making use of either religion or racial sentiment to achieve political ends or mercantile purposes. I have no respect for such motives. I do not charge the government with having had such motives in view. I have quoted from the remarks made last year by the Prime Minister to the contrary. The previous administration made a mistake in 1927 when by a very feeble act they acted upon the telegraphic order from Mr. Amery. In the present instance I am afraid the government has not resisted the temptation of gathering a little cheap success in the province of Quebec. All parties have done it at turns, and I do not brand such action as a crime. However I thought it my duty to bring the matter before the house. Having been interested in the affairs of the nation for forty years I want to warn my people in the proyince of Quebec against the delusion that

Embargo on Rxissian Goods
this little measure will have any effect whatever either in Russia, in Europe or even in Canada. It cannot have. The effect it could have had as a moral lesson has been destroyed by the simultaneous action of the government refusing to trade with Russia in certain matters but agreeing to deal with her in other matters. So much for the moral standpoint. The political lesson is lost when we think of the attitude taken by all the nations of Europe with which we are united. If it is stated that we owe a debt to our dignity I repeat that we must think of the consequences. At this point may I give an example to my Catholic friends and at the same time beg the pardon of my hon. friends who are not Catholics but who will realize my interest in raising the point?
In 1922 I was in Rome when the Genoa conference was called, the first conference following the war to which Germans and Russians were invited. Mr. Lloyd George was responsible for the convening of the conference, Mr. Briand agreed; but Mr. Poincare raised such a turmoil in the French chamber that Mr. Briand was defeated. The conference accomplished nothing for the time being but nevertheless the ice was broken. When the delegates from the nations arrived at Genoa, including Mr. Chicherin, one of the primary leaders of the bolshevic government, the venerable Cardinal Archbishop of Genoa received the delegates, including the representative of the government of Russia. The Archbishop shook hands with the delegates and appealed for the blessing of God on their deliberations for peace. Immediately some French Catholics raised their hands in horror. I am afraid some of them were more concerned with their unredeemed loans to Russia than their religious principles, because their protest was upheld by men such as Mr. Poincare and others, who had no connection whatever with Catholicism or Christianity. Those French Catholics criticized the Archbishop of Genoa for having shaken hands with the representatives of the murderous government of Russia. On the other hand however, the pope,'-the same pope who condemns communism, who condemns socialism, who protested against the crimes of Russia when all the governments of Europe were simply concerned with trying to make bargains with Russia,-the pope wrote a letter to the Archbishop of Genoa congratulating him for having gone to meet the men who were convening the first time for the purpose of establishing peace. Could not our Catholic friends in Canada have some degree of the breadth of mind and wisdom of judgment of the Roman
authorities? I am always surprised by some of the attacks made against the pope in the non-Catholic papers of Canada. They ought to know that the pope is bigger and broader minded than many Catholics in this country.
Mr. LaVERGNE: Hear, hear.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT BY ORDER IN COUNCIL-AMENDMENT, MR. BOURASSA
speechtext:
The authorities in Rome *are strict on matters of principle; t'he pope will suffer anything rather than sacrifice one principle. He will condemn communism in Russia, Canada or the United States, because he believes the principles of communism are incompatible with those of Christian social philosophy. But when it comes to dealing with men, the pope tries to make use of what is good in the sinner. Pope Pius IX has been the strongest opponent of revolution in Europe during the last century. But one day a French royalist was talking to him of the curses of the great revolution in France. To which the author of the syllabus and of so many condemnations of socialism and even of liberalism replied: "There is no such thing as absolute evil; there is only absolute good and absolute truth, and that is God himself. Even some good arose from the French revolution." The question was asked, "But, holy father, what can you point out that was good?" "Equality of all men before the law" replied Pope Pius IX.
Purely by hazard I was reading last week the very interesting memoirs of a Russian royalist who entered Russia in disguise three years ago to find out what had become of his son who had disappeared with the army of Dettekin during one of the attempts to throw down the bolshevik government. The author of the book, who himself is a royalist, entered into communications with the hidden royalists of Russia. He hopes for the downfall of the present regime and predicts the restoration sooner or later of czardom in Russia, but his conclusion is that the first duty of the restored monarchy will be to maintain all it can of what good has been accomplished by the present government in Russia. I am not revising or opposing this judgment, I am simply saying this: ignorant as we are of what is going on in Russia, incapable as we are of doing anything practical to save our traditions or our principles or our notions of social order in Russia, for heaven's sake let us mind our own affairs, and introduce into Canadian .policy, Canadian business and Canadian social arrangements some of the principles of Christianity. I think thereby we shall render a much better service both to religion and to society than by simply uttering empty words.

In conclusion, Mr. Speaker. I beg to move, seconded by Mr. Neill the following amendment:
That all the words after "that" be struck out and the following words substituted therefor:
the house regards the growing practice of deciding by order in council important matters of public policy as an encroachment upon the duties and privileges of parliament and a violation of the principle of responsible government.
